title: Shuffled Signs
statement: A sign painter reuses the letter tiles from an old shop sign to build a new one. Given the old sign first and the new sign second, both written in lowercase letters, return true if second uses exactly the same tiles as first, every tile used once, rearranged in any order. Return false otherwise.

examples.explanation: Both use one each of e, i, l, n, s, t.
The new sign needs a c and has no t.

hints.content: Two signs match when every letter appears the same number of times in both.
Different lengths mean the answer is false immediately.
Sorting both strings and comparing works, but costs n log n.
There are only 26 possible letters, so a fixed-size count array is enough.
Add one for each letter of first and subtract one for each letter of second; every count must end at zero.

testCases.explanation: Both use one each of e, i, l, n, s, t.
The new sign needs a c and has no t.
Two empty signs use the same (no) tiles.
A full reversal is a valid rearrangement.
Repeated tiles are matched by count.

solutions.title: Sort both and compare
solutions.intuition: Rearrangements of the same tiles become identical once sorted.
solutions.approach: Split each string into characters, sort, join, and compare.
commonMistakes: Comparing arrays with === instead of joined strings.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Sorting puts any rearrangement into the same canonical form. It's short and clear but pays for a sort.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: The strings are equal, so return true.

solutions.title: Count letters in one array
solutions.intuition: Only letter counts matter, and there are just 26 letters.
solutions.approach: Return false on different lengths. Walk both strings together, incrementing the count for first's letter and decrementing for second's. Return whether every count is zero.
solutions.pseudocode:
if lengths differ: return false
counts[26] = 0; for i: counts[first[i]]++; counts[second[i]]--
return all counts == 0
commonMistakes: Skipping the length check and walking past the end of the shorter string.
Using a Map when a fixed 26-slot array is simpler and faster.
solutions.interviewExplanation: With a fixed alphabet I keep one array of 26 counters, adding for the first sign and subtracting for the second. Equal multisets leave all zeros. Linear time and constant space. For Unicode text I'd switch to a Map keyed by code point.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: Lengths match (6). After processing both strings, each of e, i, l, n, s, t was added once and removed once.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Every counter is 0, so return true.
